title: Karana: keeping records, remembering Odisha
lead: A land account, a royal order and a temple inventory preserve different parts of a society’s memory. Karana histories lead into this work of recording—and into the harder question of how an inherited occupation and a community came to be associated.
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs.text: The Bhadrak district gazetteer describes Karanas writing charters and documents and serving government and zamindars as clerks, accountants and officials. It connects remuneration in unassessed land with some becoming landlords. This is a regional historical explanation; the passage does not supply an individual grant or establish when the whole community formed.
paragraphs.locator: Printed32–33; historical synthesis, no individual charter inspected

paragraphs.text: The same account places writing within a changing material world: palm leaves and iron pens, zamindari land records, then quills, locally prepared ink and paper during British rule. These are regional writing practices, not techniques exclusive to Karanas. They help us imagine the practical work behind an occupational label.

sections.title: What an old classification can tell us

paragraphs.text: In his 1825 account of Orissa Proper or Cuttack, Andrew Stirling placed “Mainti” and “Carana” alongside a description of writers or secretaries. The table is a dated outsider’s classification. Its names cannot serve as a modern alias dictionary, and its surrounding hierarchy is not a genealogy or a measure of anyone’s abilities.
paragraphs.locator: Printed172 table; attribution printed169; critical reading

sections.title: Puri: the work of keeping a chronicle

paragraphs.text: Rajata Kanta Dash’s 2022 discussion of the Madala Panji connects Karana recordkeepers with Puri’s temple chronicle. Its scope extended beyond royal succession to inventories, ceremonial routines and royal orders. The Desa Khanja section concerned temple land grants and property. Keeping institutional memory meant recording resources and obligations as well as remembered events.

Dash recounts a tradition of twenty-four Karana families, with five entrusted with writing and preserving the chronicle through Panjia, Tadau, Deula, Kotha and Baithi duties. He also says the chronicle’s actual starting date is unknown before describing its traditional attribution to Chodaganga. That foundation narrative concerns temple service; it does not establish that a king created the entire Karana community.
paragraphs.locator: pp63–64; tradition distinguished from established chronology

paragraphs.text: The chronicle survives through variant accounts and stories shaped by legend. Its manuscripts and earlier editions therefore require comparison, rather than treating every passage as a contemporary record. The underlying manuscripts were not independently inspected for this article.
paragraphs.locator: pp63–64; textual variation and direct-access limit

paragraphs.text: The Central Institute of Indian Languages’ Bhasha Sanchika catalogue records a 2020 Odia edition of the Madala Panji, edited by Artaballabh Mohanti and published by Odisha Sahitya Akademi. This is evidence of continued publication and preservation. The catalogue was inspected here, not the book’s full text.
paragraphs.locator: Full catalogue metadata: issued2020, editor, publisher, type

paragraphs.text: These sources explain an association with record-keeping more securely than they explain the beginnings of every Karana family. A fuller history needs dated service records, settlement histories and family accounts, with attention to who could learn the work and how careers changed. Neither a surname nor a similar office title can settle those questions.

For Odia heritage, the records themselves matter: they can preserve the names of places, the uses of land and the organisation of ceremonies. Reading them carefully allows inherited knowledge to remain part of public memory without making an ancestral occupation an obligation for descendants.
